analysis.one_liner: Strips federal tax breaks from corporations owning 50 or more single-family rental homes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee after a single Banking Committee hearing, with no floor action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would deny federal income tax deductions for mortgage interest and for depreciation to any taxpayer that owns 50 or more single-family rental houses. The point is to make large corporate landlords less able to use borrowed money and tax write-offs to outbid families trying to buy a home. Owners who sell a house to a family that will live in it, or to a nonprofit affordable-housing group, could claim the deductions for the year of sale.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters in corporate-owned single-family homes and families trying to buy a first home, who would face less competition from heavily financed institutional buyers. Nonprofit affordable-housing organizations, land banks, community land trusts, and resident-owned cooperatives get a defined buyer category, since sales to them would still allow the deductions.

how_it_helps.text: Disallows the mortgage interest deduction on single-family rental homes for any taxpayer that owns 50 or more of them, directly or through affiliated entities.
Also disallows depreciation deductions on those properties for large owners, so both major tax write-offs of rental real estate are off the table for them.
Treats all companies under common ownership or control as a single taxpayer, so splitting a portfolio across subsidiaries does not get under the 50-house threshold.

Preserves the deductions for a large owner in the year it sells a home to an individual who will occupy it as a primary residence, or to a qualified nonprofit such as a community land trust or land bank, encouraging sales into ownership rather than to another investor.
Excludes newly built homes from the definition, so the penalty does not apply to landlords who construct new housing.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporate and institutional owners of single-family rental homes, who would pay more federal tax on their portfolios, and potentially their lenders and investors, whose loans to these landlords would no longer generate deductions for the borrowers.

drawbacks.text: Critics of this approach argue that a large landlord facing sharply higher tax costs may pass some of it to the tenants of the affected homes through rents or reduced maintenance, at least until the properties are sold.

The bill targets only owners of 50 or more single-family rentals, so the many smaller landlords who own the bulk of single-family rentals are untouched, and a large owner can shed houses until it falls under the threshold and keep the deductions on the rest.

Denying interest deductions penalizes financing itself, which some economists would say is a blunt instrument: it could reduce rental supply in tight markets before any offsetting increase in homeownership appears.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For aspiring homebuyers and renters facing corporate competition for starter homes, the upside is real: the bill removes the two main tax write-offs that make leveraged single-family accumulation cheaper, and it steers divestment toward owner-occupants and nonprofits rather than other investors. The costs fall on large landlords and their investors, though honest supporters should acknowledge the risk of short-term rent pressure on affected tenants and the design gaps around the 50-house threshold and smaller landlords.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee at introduction, a related Senate Banking Committee held one hearing on it a year later, and the Finance Committee never reported it or brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sherrod Brown introduced the Stop Predatory Investing Act on July 11, 2023, joined by 12 original cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which held no markup and produced no vote.
On April 18, 2024, the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee held a hearing at which the bill's subject matter was discussed, with the hearing printed as S.Hrg. 118-712.
No further action followed, and the bill expired at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporate and institutional owners of single-family rental homes, who keep the interest and depreciation deductions the bill would have taken away, and any industry actors who would have faced similar measures modeled on it.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-OH); bill sponsor; Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and chaired the April 2024 Senate Banking Committee hearing at which the issue was examined; the Finance Committee, which held the bill, never acted on it.

for.name: 11 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate independents
for.role: Cosponsors, including the Senate Finance Committee chairman

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral for the remainder of the Congress without a markup, a report, or a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on and no Republican support is recorded in the action history.

industries.industry: Large corporate and institutional single-family rental owners
industries.note: These owners earn by accumulating single-family homes as rentals, financed with debt whose interest is currently deductible; the bill would raise their tax bill and, in the bill's design, push them to sell to families or nonprofits. Their gain in today's system comes at the expense of buyers priced out of ownership.

Falling under the 50-house threshold, they would keep the interest and depreciation deductions while large competitors lost them, improving their relative position. The bill does not otherwise change how they operate.
Homes a taxpayer built or acquired right after construction are excluded from the denial, so the bill keeps the tax treatment that supports building new housing rather than buying up existing homes.
